title: Salt, Fat, Acid, Heat

learn.summary: Samin Nosrat's four elements explain why food tastes good: salt amplifies flavor, fat carries it and creates texture, acid balances and brightens, heat transforms. When a dish tastes flat, the answer is almost always more salt or a splash of acid — not more spices. Internalize this framework and every recipe becomes a variation on themes you already understand.

do: Next time a dish tastes dull, fix it in two steps: add a pinch of salt, taste, then add a squeeze of lemon or splash of vinegar, taste again — name which one did more

children.title: Seasoning in Layers

learn.summary: Salt added during cooking penetrates and seasons from within; salt dumped on at the end just sits on the surface. Season at every stage — the onions as they sweat, the pasta water (it should taste like the sea, roughly 1% salt), the meat well before it hits the pan. Use kosher salt for control, and know your brand: Diamond Crystal is about half as salty by volume as Morton.

do: Cook the same simple soup or sauté twice this week: once salting only at the end, once salting at each stage — taste them side by side

children.title: Cooking Fats

learn.summary: Match the fat to the heat: butter burns around 350°F but brings flavor and browning to gentle work; extra-virgin olive oil handles moderate sautéing (roughly 375-405°F smoke point) and finishing; neutral oils like canola, grapeseed, and avocado take high-heat searing at 400-500°F. Fat is also texture — crisp, creamy, tender all come from fat handled well. When oil smokes hard, it is degrading: start over.

do: Fry two eggs tonight, one in butter over medium-low and one in olive oil over medium-high, and note the difference in edges, flavor, and browning

children.title: Acid to Finish

learn.summary: Acid is the most underused element in home kitchens: a squeeze of lemon, a splash of vinegar, or a spoon of yogurt added at the end makes rich food taste lighter and flat food taste alive. Nearly every classic cuisine finishes with acid — lime on tacos, vinegar in ramen, lemon on schnitzel. Add it off the heat and in small increments, tasting as you go.

do: Finish three different dishes this week with acid — lemon on roasted vegetables, vinegar in a soup, lime on rice — and note which transformation surprises you most

children.title: Taste Constantly

learn.summary: Professionals taste dozens of times per dish; home cooks often taste once, at the table, when it is too late. Keep a spoon by the stove and taste at every stage: after salting, after adding acid, before serving. Ask two questions each time — does it need salt, and does it need acid? — and you will out-cook most recipe followers within a month.

do: Put a cup of teaspoons next to your stove tonight and taste your next dish at least five times while cooking it, adjusting after each taste
